reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / DeVita's Cancer: Principles & Practice of Oncology
clinicalPearls: Thymomas are the most common tumours of the anterior mediastinum in adults and are frequently discovered incidentally on chest imaging

There is a strong association with myasthenia gravis, and a proportion of patients present first with neuromuscular symptoms; other paraneoplastic syndromes include pure red cell aplasia and hypogammaglobulinaemia
Local symptoms, when present, arise from mass effect and include chest pain, cough, dyspnoea, and features of superior vena cava obstruction
Thymic carcinoma is a distinct and more aggressive entity than thymoma, with greater invasiveness, higher metastatic potential, and worse prognosis
Staging emphasises the degree of local invasion beyond the capsule and into surrounding structures, which is the main determinant of behaviour and treatment
Complete surgical resection is the cornerstone of treatment for resectable disease, and completeness of resection strongly influences outcome
Radiotherapy is used adjuvantly for invasive or incompletely resected tumours, and chemotherapy, often platinum-based, is used for advanced or unresectable disease
Patients with associated myasthenia gravis require optimisation of neuromuscular status before surgery to reduce perioperative respiratory risk
reference.pathophysiology: Thymomas are neoplasms of the thymic epithelial cells, typically accompanied by variable numbers of non-neoplastic immature T lymphocytes. They are classified histologically by epithelial morphology and lymphocyte content, while thymic carcinoma shows overt cytological malignancy and loss of organotypic features. The abnormal thymic microenvironment can disrupt immune tolerance, accounting for the frequent paraneoplastic autoimmune phenomena, most notably myasthenia gravis mediated by anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies. Tumours may remain encapsulated or invade the capsule, mediastinal fat, pleura, pericardium, and adjacent great vessels.
additionalDifferentials: Germ cell tumour of the mediastinum
Parathyroid adenoma or other mediastinal masses
additionalInvestigations: Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest to characterise the anterior mediastinal mass and local invasion
MRI to clarify cystic versus solid components and vascular involvement
Testing for anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies and evaluation for myasthenia gravis
Full blood count and immunoglobulin levels to detect associated red cell aplasia or hypogammaglobulinaemia
Biopsy when the diagnosis is uncertain or the tumour appears unresectable, and PET-CT for suspected thymic carcinoma
redFlags: Superior vena cava obstruction with facial swelling and distended neck veins
Respiratory compromise or myasthenic crisis in a patient with a mediastinal mass
Rapidly enlarging or invasive anterior mediastinal mass suggesting thymic carcinoma
New pleural or pericardial effusion indicating advanced spread
reference.prognosis: Encapsulated, completely resected thymomas have an excellent long-term prognosis, whereas invasive tumours and especially thymic carcinoma carry higher recurrence and mortality; degree of invasion and completeness of resection are the key prognostic factors.
pitfalls: Overlooking underlying myasthenia gravis and precipitating perioperative respiratory failure
Failing to distinguish aggressive thymic carcinoma from indolent thymoma
Biopsying a potentially resectable encapsulated tumour when upfront resection is preferable
Missing associated paraneoplastic cytopenias or immunodeficiency
references: DeVita's Cancer: Principles & Practice of Oncology
management: Manage thymoma with multidisciplinary input from thoracic surgery, radiation oncology, and medical oncology, since surgery, radiation, and systemic therapy may each play a role depending on stage.

For early-stage (Masaoka I/II) disease, complete R0 surgical resection via open or minimally invasive thymectomy is the mainstay of therapy and the strongest predictor of long-term survival; complete thymectomy is preferred over partial resection.

Postoperative radiation is not recommended after complete resection of stage I disease; for stage II disease the evidence is mixed and radiation is an individualized decision based on margin status and histology.
Chemotherapy, targeted therapy, or immunotherapy is almost never indicated for stage I/II thymoma.
For locally advanced disease (Masaoka III/IV), pursue extended resection when feasible, since even incomplete resection appears to improve survival compared with biopsy alone.

Use radiation therapy after incomplete resection or for unresectable locally advanced disease, and consider platinum-based combination chemotherapy (commonly a platinum plus anthracycline backbone) as neoadjuvant, postoperative, or definitive treatment.

A multimodality sequence of induction chemotherapy, surgery, and adjuvant radiation can be used for stage III/IV disease, with concurrent chemoradiotherapy as an option when resection is not feasible.

For recurrent, refractory, or metastatic disease, consider repeat resection, multikinase/angiogenesis-targeted tyrosine kinase inhibitors, mTOR inhibition, or somatostatin analogs as second-line options.

Reserve immune checkpoint inhibition for thymoma only with specialist oversight, given the substantial risk of triggering or worsening autoimmune paraneoplastic syndromes, especially with a history of myasthenia gravis.

Actively screen for myasthenia gravis and other paraneoplastic syndromes (pure red cell aplasia, hypogammaglobulinemia/Good syndrome), since their presence affects perioperative risk and requires co-management with neurology, hematology, or immunology.
Avoid needle biopsy when thymoma is suspected; refer for multidisciplinary evaluation and surgical planning before any biopsy or resection.

For thymic carcinoma, favor an aggressive multimodality approach with resection plus postoperative radiation and chemotherapy when resectable, and consider neoadjuvant chemotherapy to improve resectability.

Follow resected thymoma patients long-term with periodic clinical assessment and chest imaging, since recurrence can occur locally or in the pleura even years later; the exact surveillance interval should be set by the treating multidisciplinary team.
Refer locally advanced, unresectable, recurrent, or metastatic disease to a center experienced in multimodality thymic tumor management.
